name: London wedge (c3-d4-e3 with the dark-squared bishop outside)

plans.label: Clamp a knight on e5
plans.description: The wedge exists to make e5 usable: White's own d4 pawn guards that square, so a knight landing there is pawn-supported and can be removed only by a trade or by a Black pawn move that costs something. Build behind it — the queen's knight to d2, the light bishop to d3 — and jump last.

success.note: A White knight stands on e5 with the c3 and d4 pawns still behind it. Whether it is achieving anything there is not a census fact.

plans.label: Recapture toward the h-file
plans.description: When Black hunts the outside bishop with a knight, step to g3 and let the trade happen: the h-pawn recaptures inward, the g-pawns double, and no White pawn is left on the h-file for the rook standing behind it.

success.note: White's g-pawns are doubled and White has no h-pawn — the trade landed on g3. The census cannot say whether the rook ever uses the file.

plans.label: Unlock the wedge with e3-e4
plans.description: The wedge is scaffolding, not a destination. Once the pieces are placed, e3-e4 turns the buried pawn into a second central pawn, empties the file behind it, and asks Black's d5 pawn what it intends to do.

success.note: White has pawns on d4 and e4 and none on e3. The census cannot tell which pawn arrived on e4, nor whether the break was timed well.

plans.label: Trade the c-pawn and take the file
plans.description: Black's counterplay runs down the c-file: challenge d4 with the c-pawn, then resolve the tension so that no Black pawn is left on that file. The file, not the trade, is the point.

success.note: No Black pawn stands on the c-file while White's d4 pawn still does. Whether Black's rooks arrive in time is not a census fact.

plans.label: Send the bill to b2
plans.description: A bishop standing outside on f4 or g3 is a bishop not standing on c1, and the queen's knight has usually gone to d2 rather than c3. Black's queen to b6, a knight to a5 and a rook to b8 ask White to answer for the square the bishop left.

success.note: White's b2 pawn is attacked and no White piece defends it. Whether it can safely be taken is a different question, and not one a census answers.

plans.label: Trade the wedge bishop off
plans.description: The wedge is built around one bishop: put a bishop opposite it and offer the trade until it is gone, leaving the pawn wedge without the piece it was built around.

success.note: RESTATED PLAN. The plan was 'Challenge the outside bishop' — trade it or hunt it — and its success covered both plus the tempo ledger. It is now the trade alone: the c3/d4/e3 wedge still stands and White's dark-squared bishop, the piece it was built around, is off the board. Because bishops never change shade, this distinguishes a traded bishop from one that merely retreated. The hunt's tempo cost is still unpriced. Original success note: 'Detection cannot tell a traded bishop from one that simply moved away, and cannot price the tempi the hunt cost either side.'

plans.label: Fianchetto the light-squared bishop
plans.description: The other answer to the bishop stuck behind the e-pawn: give it the long diagonal with the b-pawn and b7, and time the central break for the moment the diagonal actually opens. In this structure Black's d5 pawn is the last blocker and it only leaves when White breaks with the c- or e-pawn.

success.note: Black's bishop stands on b7 with the e6 pawn placed and no Black pawn left on d5. What stands beyond d5 the signature does not count.

plans.label: Free the light-squared bishop first
plans.description: Black's central pawns on d5 and e6 stand on light squares, so Black owns White's problem in mirror image. Get the queen's bishop to f5 or g4 before the e-pawn shuts its diagonal, and the wedge is met by a fully developed opponent.

success.note: Black's light-squared bishop stands on f5 or g4 while the d5 and e6 pawns are placed. The census cannot certify that the move order was chosen rather than lucky.

watch: c3, d4 and e3 are all dark squares. The wedge stands on exactly the colour White's dark-squared bishop travels, which is the entire reason that bishop is developed before the e-pawn moves and not after.

How many pieces actually defend b2 once the bishop is outside and the queen's knight sits on d2. Across all fourteen positions where this entry fires in the two shipped London packs, the answer is none. CORRECTED 2026-08-16 (D379): this entry now fires on nineteen positions across three packs, not fourteen across two. The answer is still none - zero White defenders of b2 at every one of the nineteen.
The attacker and defender count on d4 as the c-pawn, the queen's knight and the queen arrive: the wedge holds exactly as long as the arithmetic does.
Which side's problem bishop gets out first — White's dark-squared one before e3, or Black's light-squared one before the e-pawn moves.
Whether e3-e4 ever actually happens. A wedge that never breaks is a wall White is also living behind.
typicalMistakes: Playing e3 while the dark-squared bishop is still on c1: with White pawns on b2 and e3, a bishop on c1 has exactly one legal destination, d2.
As Black, playing the e-pawn to e6 while the queen's bishop is still on c8 — the mirror of White's own mistake, with the same one-square consequence.
Treating the wedge as a finished position rather than a construction: the same six moves against every Black setup, with no plan for either the e5 outpost or the e4 break.
Taking on b2 because the census says the pawn is undefended. Undefended is a board fact; free is a calculation.
Retreating the outside bishop from a knight instead of stepping to g3 and letting the trade pay for the h-file.

sources: COMMISSIONED by the wave-4a opening batch: content/drafts/london-system-white.json and content/drafts/anti-london-black.json both record in graduationBlockers that they ship with NO shapes reference deliberately, because no library entry named the London wedge and the authors declined to point at a wrong one. This entry is the commissioned structure; those two packs are its first customers.

MECHANICALLY DERIVED (this session) with the repo's own evaluator — packages/runtime/src/structure.ts matchesStructuralExpression, bundled through the repo's esbuild and driven over positions walked with the repo's chessops dependency. Firing census over all 487 spine positions of the 37 shipped packs in content/drafts: this trigger fires on exactly 14 nodes, the seven from p11-c3 to p17-ne5 in each of the two London packs, and nowhere else in the corpus. It is false at the standard initial position. RE-DERIVED 2026-08-16 (D379) with `make expression-census` plus a spine walk over the current corpus - 827 authored spine positions across 56 packs under content/drafts and content/packs - and it is the PROPOSITION that changed, not only the numerals: this trigger fires on 19 nodes across THREE packs, so 'and nowhere else in the corpus' is false and is withdrawn. The reading is anti-london-black 7 and london-system-white 7, both still exactly p11-c3 p12-bd6 p13-bg3 p14-o-o p15-bd3 p16-b6 p17-ne5 as the sentence above says, plus london-wedge-black-counterplay 5 (start b6-fianchetto ne5-clamp-early bb7-diagonal f4-stonewall), a pack that did not exist when this line was written and whose own start position already stands inside the wedge. So 487 -> 827 and 14 -> 19, and the two named packs' own counts did not move: the whole increase is the third pack. Still false at the standard initial position, re-checked.

MECHANICALLY DERIVED (this session), the facts the prose states as facts: (1) c3, d4, e3, b2, f4, g3, h2, c1 and d2 are all dark squares, by shade arithmetic; (2) with White pawns on b2 and e3, a bishop on c1 has exactly one legal destination, d2 — enumerated on a bare test position and again on a Colle-style position; the mirror enumeration in the anti-London tabiya after Black has played the e-pawn to e6 gives the c8 bishop exactly one destination, d7; (3) a White pawn on d4 attacks c5 and e5, which is what supports the e5 outpost; (4) at every one of the 14 firing nodes, White's b2 pawn has zero White defenders, and d4 has three White defenders against two Black attackers (two against two after the knight reaches e5). RE-DERIVED 2026-08-16 (D379): items (1) to (3) re-check unchanged - the nine named squares are all dark by shade arithmetic; the c1 bishop still enumerates exactly one destination, d2, on the bare test position and on the Colle-style one; the mirror enumeration after Black plays the e-pawn to e6 still gives the c8 bishop exactly one, d7; and a White pawn on d4 still attacks c5 and e5. Item (4) is now measured over the 19 firing nodes rather than 14, and its substance holds at every one: b2 has zero White defenders at all 19, and d4 reads three White defenders against two Black attackers at 14 of them and two against two at the other five - which are exactly the five carrying a White knight on e5 (p17-ne5 of both original packs, and ne5-clamp-early, bb7-diagonal and f4-stonewall of london-wedge-black-counterplay), so the parenthesis is still a rule and not a coincidence of the old sample.

MECHANICALLY DERIVED (this session), plan success signatures: each non-null signature was evaluated on a legally reached position that satisfies it and on a reference position that does not. The e5 clamp fires at p17-ne5 of both packs (RE-DERIVED 2026-08-16, D379: still true, and the same signature now fires 6 times across three packs - those two nodes plus ne5-clamp, ne5-clamp-early, bb7-diagonal and f4-stonewall of london-wedge-black-counterplay); the h-file signature after a knight-for-bishop trade recaptured with the h-pawn; the e4 break after a constructed continuation; the c-file signature after the c-pawns are traded off, and separately confirmed to be satisfiable while the wedge itself is still standing; the b2 signature after the black queen arrives on b6; the free-the-bishop-first signature on a line where that bishop leaves before the e-pawn moves, and false on the line where it does not; the b7 fianchetto signature false while Black's d5 pawn stands and true once White's e-pawn break removes it.

MECHANICALLY DERIVED (this session), and it is why the b7 plan reads as it does: in this structure Black's d5 pawn has no capture available while White's pawns sit on c3 and e3, so it leaves only when White plays c4 or e4 first. A continuation was walked to confirm the plan's success condition is reachable at all rather than decorative.

REFUTES an authored claim in a customer pack. content/drafts/anti-london-black.json planClasses b2-counterattack said the bishop's departure from c1 leaves b2 'attended only by the queen'. Counted with this repo's direct_attack_count at the pack's own deviation position, reached by 1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bf4 c5 4.e3 Qb6: White pieces bearing on b2 = 0. The queen on d1 does not attack b2 on any line. With the bishop still on c1 the count is 1, and that one is the bishop. The pack's wording was corrected in the same session; this entry's own b2 plan states the zero-defender fact instead.

TRIGGER SCOPE, stated rather than implied. The dark-squared bishop is required to stand on f4, g3 or h2 — the squares of its own b8-h2 diagonal outside the wedge. Verified consequences: a Colle setup (identical pawns, bishop still on c1) does NOT fire, and a Torre setup (bishop on g5) does NOT fire, both checked on constructed positions. Londons played without the c3 pawn, and Jobava-style setups with a knight on c3 instead of a pawn, also do not fire. Those are separate structures with different plan ownership and each needs its own entry if it is wanted; this entry does not claim them.

UNGROUNDED: every strategic claim here — all six plan descriptions, the non-derived watch items and typical mistakes, and every judgment about what a plan is worth — is agent-authored prose with no citation, no engine evaluation, no corpus frequency and no human review. What is machine-derived is labelled above; everything else is assertion.
